Where in the paper: Table III (mean values for the intense vorticity structures, one row per simulation); Table II (\(\nu\) in code units); definitions in Sec. III, Eq. (8)–(10).

What was measured, and how the tubes were picked: The structures are the points with the highest vorticity magnitude, 1% of the volume (the intense vorticity structures, IVS); the radius is where the azimuthal mean of the axial vorticity has fallen to \(1/e\) of its axis value.

8
Remarks in the page: Their \(\Gamma_{ivs}=2\pi\langle U_{ivs}\rangle R_{ivs}\) (Eq. 9) is the circulation inside \(R_{ivs}\), about 61% of the total of a Burgers vortex, and is about 0.83 of \(2\pi U_{ivs}R_{ivs}\) from the same table (162 against 136 at \(Re_\lambda=90\)), probably because the paper averages the product per structure. The total circulation is therefore taken from the converted radius and swirl, \(\Gamma/\nu=8.78\,Re_c\) with \(Re_c=(r_{\max}/\eta)(U_{\max}/U_\eta)\); the listed \(Re_\Gamma Re_\lambda^{-1/2}\) is kept in the table as the source value. The swirl row converts the swirl listed at \(R_{ivs}\) to the Burgers peak; the tubes are intense, so \(Re_c\) is about twice that of the whole tubes.

3. The conversions
10
$$r_{\max}=\sqrt{x}\,R_B=1.12\,\dfrac{R_{ivs}}{R_{ivs}/R_B}$$
11
$$\dfrac{\Gamma}{\nu}=\dfrac{2\pi}{K_B}\,Re_c=8.78\,\dfrac{r_{\max}}{\eta}\dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}\qquad(\text{total circulation from the converted radius and swirl; the listed }Re_\Gamma\text{ is not used})$$
12
$$\dfrac{U_{\max}}{U_\eta}=\dfrac{U_{ivs}/u_\eta}{f(k)},\quad k=\dfrac{R_{ivs}/R_B}{\sqrt{x}},\quad f(k)=\dfrac{1-e^{-xk^2}}{k\,(1-e^{-x})}$$
13
The Burgers vortex: \(x=1.2564312\) is the root of \(e^{x}-2x-1=0\), \(K_B=1-e^{-x}=0.71531\), \(r_{\max}=\sqrt{x}\,R_B=1.1209\,R_B\), \(U_{\max}=K_B\,\Gamma/(2\pi r_{\max})\), so \(\Gamma/\nu=(2\pi/K_B)\,Re_c=8.784\,Re_c\) with \(Re_c=r_{\max}U_{\max}/\nu\).

Worked example, the first row (\(Re_\lambda\) = 90). The model side needs lengths in metres, so \(\eta\) is made from a \(\nu\) and an \(\varepsilon\) (reference values: [GUESS: water, ν = 1e-6 m²/s, ε = 0.1 W/kg — because the paper's flow has no physical units, and the page converts every length given in η with these reference values]):
17
$$\eta=\left(\frac{\nu^3}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/4}=\left(\frac{(1e-06)^3}{0.1}\right)^{1/4}=5.623e-05\ \mathrm{m}=56.23\ \mu\mathrm{m}$$
18
$$U_\eta=(\nu\varepsilon)^{1/4}=0.01778\ \mathrm{m/s}=17.78\ \mathrm{mm/s}$$
19
$$r_{\max}=\beta\,\eta=4.993\times56.23\ \mu\mathrm{m}=280.8\ \mu\mathrm{m}$$
20
$$U_{\max}=U\,U_\eta=3.669\times17.78\ \mathrm{mm/s}=65.25\ \mathrm{mm/s}$$
21
$$\gamma=\frac{4x}{\beta^2}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\nu}\right)^{1/2}=\frac{4\times1.2564}{4.993^2}\left(\frac{0.1}{1e-06}\right)^{1/2}=63.74\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$$

7. Digitising the pdf
31
The pdf is drawn with a logarithmic vertical axis, and the curves of the figure are a band (several curves). The digitiser finds, at each horizontal position, the upper bound and the lower bound of the plotted curves, and takes \(P=(P_{top}+P_{bottom})/2\). The pixel rows are turned into values with the tick marks of the axis: \(\log_{10}P = \text{top exponent} - \dfrac{y-y_0}{y_1-y_0}\times\text{decades}\) (a straight line on the logarithmic axis, fixed by two labelled ticks).
32
Rules of the digitiser: the points where the lower bound is below 2×10⁻⁴ are dropped (those are the noisy single-count tail lines of the figure); the curve starts at the first point above that and ends where the band falls to the floor of the plot.

8. The radius, and the fit with two lognormals
37
The radius of maximum swirl is half the diameter: \(r_{\max}=D/2\), so \(p_r(r)=2\,p_D(2r)\). The curve is scaled to a total area of 1 (the digitised area, the rise below the first point and the tail beyond the last point are all counted: summary_pdfs.normalise). A single lognormal does not fit (the curve has a narrow core and a long tail), so two are fitted in the linear domain (a fit in log P weights the tail as much as the core, and the core is what we need), with the weight free, the medians ordered \(\mu_2>\mu_1\) and \(s_2\ge2s_1\) as you asked.
38
The fit to the diameter pdf (older figure: the bimodal fit and its two components).
39
$$p(x)=a_1\,\frac{e^{-(\ln x-\mu_1)^2/2s_1^2}}{x\,s_1\sqrt{2\pi}}+(1-a_1)\,\frac{e^{-(\ln x-\mu_2)^2/2s_2^2}}{x\,s_2\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad \text{median}=e^{\mu},\quad \text{mode}=e^{\mu-s^2},\quad \text{mean}=e^{\mu+s^2/2}$$

3. How the eddies are found
8
The identification of the paper: the local flow pattern, no threshold.
9
The scheme (from the text): Q of the velocity gradient tensor at each collocation point; the probability that a positive maximum of Q lies near each point; the points with high probability are searched with a 3-D fourth-order Lagrange interpolation for the true maximum; a plane normal to the vorticity vector through the maximum gives the mean azimuthal velocity, and the point of minimum variance of the azimuthal velocity is searched around it. The radius is where the mean azimuthal velocity is maximal; \(\eta\) and \(u_K\) are those 'calculated from mean energy dissipation rate at \(y^+\), where the eddy exists'.

At \(y^+\approx145\) the dissipation reads \(\varepsilon^+\approx0.015\) [GUESS: ε⁺ ≈ 0.015 at y⁺ = 145 — because read by eye from Fig. 3, to ±10 %], so \(\eta^+\approx2.9\). At \(Re_\tau=800\): \(\Delta x/\eta=9.82/2.9=3.4\), \(\Delta z/\eta=6.54/2.9=2.3\); at \(Re_\tau=180\): 4.1 and 2.4. \(\Delta/\eta\) depends on the wall distance (near the wall \(\varepsilon^+\) is larger, \(\eta^+\) smaller): the pdf pools all the bands, so no single number describes it.

Where in the paper: Sec. 2 (the von Kármán facility; DNS of Li et al. at \(Re_\lambda=418\)); Sec. 3.1 and the Conclusions (the mean radius); Fig. 12 and the text before it (the ratio \(R/R_B\)).

\(r_{\max}/\eta\)151–718——3.5 (text)5.5475comparisonrange
8
Remarks in the page: The method measures a time record, which the mean velocity \(U\) turns into a distance (frozen flow); the radius follows from the spacing of the two extrema of the signal as the filament passes, and the peak amplitude gives \(U_{\max}\). The value \(R=3.5\,\eta\) is the position of the maximum of the size distribution seen by the probe (Fig. 5, which collapses for \(Re_\lambda=151\)–718), quoted by the authors as the mean worm size; the same distribution built from the DNS of Jiménez et al. through the same probe geometry (their Eq. 9) peaks at 2.8 \(\eta\), so the probe sizes are 1.25 times the DNS sizes. The distribution is skewed with a tail to about 20 \(\eta\), and a rough reading of the figure puts its mean near 6 \(\eta\) and its median near 5 \(\eta\). The row uses the peak, \(r_{\max}=1.585\times3.5=5.5\,\eta\), as a range of \(Re_\lambda\). Above \(Re_\lambda\approx700\) the size distribution widens: the mean velocity increment across the filament decreases and its mean radius increases so that the circulation does not change; the authors read this as an instability of the filaments. The paper has no table of \(R\), \(U_{\max}\) or the circulation by \(Re_\lambda\).

7. Digitising: the open symbols only

The figure has filled symbols (the bands near the wall) and open symbols (the bands 110 < y⁺ < 145 and 145 < y⁺ < 180, the outer bands). You asked for the open ones only, because the others lie in the buffer region. The two high-resolution crops you gave (das2006_fig7a.png, das2006_fig7b.png) were used.
29
The high-resolution crop of panel (a), the diameter pdf.
30
Open markers are found as holes: the image is binarised, the holes of the closed marker outlines are filled, the dark pixels (the black lines and filled markers) are subtracted, and what remains is a ring. A ring with too much dark inside it (a hole between two black markers, not a marker) is rejected (annulus darkness above 0.60). The marker positions then lie on a grid of the x positions of the series: where a marker is hidden behind a black one, the expected x position is taken from the two series' spacing and the pixels there are averaged in y.
